text: I want to ask you about Verse.  You know, we end up thinking that guys who played in a 3-4 formation can switch to a 4-3 and not lose their rhythm.  But is it an adjustment for him in his system compared to what he was used to? Well, every time you change teams or systems, I imagine there's a normal adjustment process, right?  But in terms of techniques and fundamentals, he is learning very, very well.  He understands the line of attack.  He did a lot of that playing in his position for the Rams.  And you're seeing this.  And I keep seeing it every day in training.  I keep seeing it in the games, in his exit strategy, in the disruption, in containing the wing spike, and in his strength when pressuring the passer and creating chaos in the backcourt.  And this is ongoing. It seems you used the "wide nine" occasionally.  Way out there, every now and then. I mean, we're going to be a line of attack.    Does that please him? For sure.  For sure.  We're going to be a line of attack.  This is ingrained in the Cleveland Browns' defense.  We'll give it our all and try to play on their side of the line of scrimmage, no matter what.  And that 's the basis of this line.  That's why we call it an engine.  And as I tell you every week, we'll go where they go.  And I'm excited about the path they're taking. Mike, can you talk about the fact that you guys are a bit short-handed on the defensive line, in the interior?  Carson wasn't out there again today.  And how are you approaching this game with so many players on the injured list? We have the best group of guys who are full of spirit.  I mean, you see how we trained today and yesterday, there's a lot of spirit involved.  Our competitive nature is amazing.  And we have a lot of guys who play in our style.  They play for each other. They play with a lot of determination.  We are constantly trying to find different ways to create advantages. And that's the mental part.  And then, in the end, it's our fist, right?  And you see that every day from our group of guys, no matter who's on the field.  And that's the best part about being there with them and being a part of it. There is also uncertainty regarding the quarterback and who the team will face .  Lamar didn't train again today, it seems.  Hmm, when you're dealing with something like that, especially, you know, with the starter being a guy like Lamar Jackson, how do you approach preparing for the potential of either quarterback?    I mean , we're facing the Ravens.  Lamar and Snoop are both elite quarterbacks.  I mean, everything Lamar has done speaks for itself.  And you see that every time Snoop comes in, they win a lot of games.  He is highly productive.  And it's not just the quarterback, there are the great running backs Derrick Henry and Justice Hill, the tight ends, Mark Andrews has been in this for a long time.  They brought in new guys who are playing at a high level .  They have very good receivers.  The offensive line...We have to prepare for the Ravens. Todd Monken, can you give some perspective on your preparation regarding those guys you mentioned , what motivates them, and the best ways to neutralize them?  How does he fit into the game plan? You know, Monk is amazing.  Every week, I mean, he's been practicing attacks for a long time.  So, every week he brings great insights, whether about players, formations, or game situations.  He helped me, the team helped me a lot.  And, you know, it's a new offensive coaching staff there, a really good staff.  So, we have to prepare for the Ravens based on what we see in the videos, you know, and because of the great players and team they have. If Carson can't play, I think Easton will probably be the next one to step in.  What would you say to him about the situation, especially considering he plays linebacker and all?  What would you say to him about this moment and this opportunity? Just do exactly what he did during training camp.  He was amazing during Carson's absence.  I'll let Monk handle who comes in and who goes out, but whoever plays, just do what you've been doing your whole life.  And Easton had the unique experience of being on the training camp and did an incredible job.  And that's exactly what I would tell him. And what about Quincy?  Did he raise his own bar significantly with the game he played?  And what did you think of his performance? This reminds me of a time when I was asked a similar question in New York.  And for Quincy, the sky's always the limit.  I don't know if there's a defined goal for Quincy.  He keeps getting better and better.  He continues to find his rhythm with the players we have here.  It's really cool to see him with the linebacker team, Tarv, Zach Allen, Paul Worrilow, and the guys working together and gelling.  And what an incredible game he played last weekend.  I can't wait to see him continue giving great performances. And what about Sam Kamara?  I mean, I know it 's placed there.  Like, it's his first sack in six years in the league.  How did you see him persevere, you know, between training, getting promoted, and all that stuff? I mean, how cool is that, right?  And that's to Sam's credit.  You know, he bounced back after what happened in training.  You saw that in Sam.  And then he needs to recover from being away.  And he works incredibly hard.    He gets the chance and does exactly what we all expected him to do .  He plays with a lot of determination.  It gives us some really cool gifts inside the line.  And then he is rewarded for all his hard work with a great performance.  I'm very happy for him.  Sam also brings his aggressiveness.  It brings out the combative side of our style.  And we will always stick to our style and our defensive line.  And he's a huge part of what's really fun to watch. You mentioned Easton and the training camp experience he had, you know, filling in for Carson. You had a lot of players on that side, you know, on your side of the ball, who were out several times during training camp.  How much did you see that extra work the reserves had to do back then , in a way, pay off, you know, in those first five weeks? Jeff Ulbrich taught me a lesson. It was a tough training lesson being a positional coach.  I remember him telling me that the hardest position in the NFL is being a backup in the NFL.  Because you don't get the replays.  You don't receive it.  There is a limited number of repetitions .  And you need to learn from your teammate.  And it's a term we've been trying to discuss, we've been talking about. And any opportunity you have as a substitute or starter, you need to take advantage of that opportunity.  That repetition will reappear somewhere, somehow.  And our guys did an incredible job, whether it was in a replay on the field, in the OSP, or in a play from two weeks ago. Our guys did a really good job building up those repetitions . It's a great offensive line, very well trained.  And we have to prepare for the Ravens' offensive line and offense in general.    Did you do anything extra this week to train your fumble recovery ?  Or, you know, part of it was related to the atmosphere in that game?  It seemed like it was possible to recover two of them. You're being so demanding of us .  For sure.  You always want to take advantage of it whenever you force a turnover, right?  Anything, Mary Kay, in a game or in training, that we don't feel is up to our standards, we'll take care of. On the other hand, in whatever areas we feel we need to continue building, we will continue.  And that's how we approach each week. You're basically playing nickel or with three safeties.  They're not using many formations with three linebackers.  What is your philosophy for maintaining this approach instead of playing more defensively? You know, I think every week you need to figure out what the best player combinations are for what you're going to face. You adjusted, it seems, quite quickly during the game after the first drive with Garrett Wilson's 70-yard opening drive, and then neutralized him for much of the rest of the game . And in every game, whether it's the first, third, or tenth campaign, it's a constant process of all of us together on the sidelines, trying to figure out what's best for the next campaign.  And then, don't even think about anything after that. So, damn.  Whatever happens in that campaign, that's what's best for the next one.  And sometimes it's adjustments. Sometimes it's just a matter of taking a step back .  Let's let our playing style take control.  So, the way they responded is to their credit.  And also, part of it is just heart, the resilience after a difficult first campaign to turn things around .  It's a credit to our players. During this period with these tackle injuries, was there any temptation to put First on the inside? You know, I'm not going to go into detail with Tony about all the things involved in this, but I have complete confidence in him.  And we all have complete confidence in our tackles.  Whoever is out there .  They demonstrated this.  They show it every day in training.  The great advantage of what we do is that you get to see it every day.  It 's not like you go into a game thinking, "Oh, crap, I don't know what happened there."  You know exactly what it is , and the guys who are there, whether they're tackles or any other position, you get the chance to see them every day in training, individually, in practice. I'll keep things between us, you know , and within our group.  We never want to give up a touchdown, you know ?  And it doesn't matter, we simply never want to give up a touchdown. title: Saints OC Doug Nussmeier on handling pressure, run game, situations dictating play calls and more
text: So, what impresses you about the Giants' defense and how they manage to pressure their opponents without one of their main stars on the field? Well, they create pressure through aggression, you understand.  It was a big loss for them and their style of play, but they did a great job of making up for it in a sketchy way.  Of course, it's already a proven fact that their quarterback pressure numbers have increased significantly. This…this is obviously a scheme with frequent blitzes, but is this a different type of blitz compared to the ones we saw last week, or is it possible that the Forty- Niners scheme is just much more complex?    Does this sound logical? Well, you know, I wouldn't say it's more difficult. I would say they are very different, you know... Like when you say you often hear the term " West Coast attack."  And then you turn on the video and say : "They say this guy plays the West Coast style, and that guy does too." But they look completely different. These are two completely different teams.  And I'm thinking, " Hmm, so what exactly is this attack?"  So, you know, pressure comes in different types and forms, as intended by different coordinators.  To answer your question, I would say that they belong to different " families," if I may say so.    In general and simpler terms, do you agree that you will likely have to face blitzes more often until you show that you are able to respond to them better than you have in recent weeks? Yes, this takes us back to the very basics of football, right?  If you've been "exposed" under pressure, expect it to continue until you prove you can handle it. What...I understand you won't say what you'll do next, but what were you hoping to do in the last few games to counteract this, and what didn't work for you ? Well, you know, I don't think you can say, " Something didn't quite work out."  Isn't that right? Of course, there are times when you find yourself in situations like I said last week before that game, it's high risk and high reward for the defense.  So obviously we weren't able to take advantage of it as much as we had hoped. Of course, we had some bad games .  We need to avoid such unfortunate moments. So, you know, the most important thing is not to change the momentum and the course of the game, to stay in the game, wait for the right opportunity and then act. Can you name the number of "easy boxes" you encounter and what you can do to play better in such situations? Well, now you're confusing me, because we were just talking about the pressure on us, and now you're saying I'm getting "light boxing."  So, I don't...No, listen, I understand what you're saying.  So obviously when you get "easy boxes," the general idea is to run with the ball, right?  Force your opponent to create a numerical advantage, add players to the defense to outplay you.  This is a game of chess.  So obviously we continue to work on the takeaway game .  I think we had some power runs last week. We are not at that level yet .  We are working to achieve this.  We need to become better. I'm asking too simply, so excuse me, but during that 15-play touchdown drive, a lot of things on the ground looked efficient.  Why did it prove unviable or what adjustment did they make that prevented you from continuing to operate successfully? Yes, obviously, if we had the answer, we would probably have won that match.  I'm not trying to be a smartass, but this reality is a chess game you're playing.  Of course, there were moments we would have liked to replay. There were also some execution issues that we couldn't do properly.  So it's a bit of everything, really, but what we preach to our players—that's what it should look like. Here's what it might look like.  This is what we are capable of.  And we saw what we were capable of.  We need to go out, get the job done, and do it consistently. So, going back to the post-game analysis, what exactly worked in that 15-game run, what would you like to see going forward? I think the physical component of our races.  I think it was the way the players broke through.  They ran hard and we created a creative movement.  We got some great passes through gaps in the defense.  And that's exactly what you're aiming to achieve in a takeaway game. Do you see more ways to use C.J. to your advantage in the running game? Yes, you know, it was a pleasant surprise, of course.  Um, a big, physically strong guy.  You see how confident he is in defense. He's doing great.  So you see that physical strength when you watch him run with the ball. He may not have the explosive speed of some truly speedy running backs, but he is a serious physical force on the field.  He did a good job for us . How do you rate the delay penalties, especially two in the running game? It seems Fant and Donaldson got two each.  They pushed you back a little bit. How do you feel about this ?  How do you fix this? Next draw.    We must remain neutral. Listen, you'll still be charged for delays.  Whether I agree with them or not is not for me to decide.  The judges made a decision. We have great referees in this league.  They made a decision.  I do n't necessarily have to agree with all of these decisions. Um, in one case there was a delay.  As for the other thing, I would say: yes , it's football, especially when the ball is already 5 yards from the spot of the foul.  So I won't go into all those details.  But, in any case, I will say that it hurts, especially when you make an explosive run, and suddenly, as I said last week: we couldn't be at a disadvantage against them, because then you're playing right into their defensive scheme.  And when you look at the game, that's exactly what happened.  We played in disadvantageous situations too often But why do you guys say that?  You seem to be 11th in terms of third attempt success, although your first and second attempt success rate is quite low, below average.  What works on the third try that you can't just take and ...I guess it comes down to if you had the answer you would do it, but what do you think is the difference between the two? Well, you raised a valid question. You know, 40% of our third downs last week were from 11+ yards.  And you can look at the success rate depending on the attempt and the distance on the third attempt in this league. When you find yourself in a situation like this, there is little success. You know, you probably have a single-digit percentage of realization, if you look at it in dynamics and considering other things like that. So, uh, how do you put all this together?  You know, I think you strive to play a complete game where you have...I've been on teams where we lived in a world of third downs and 4 –6 yards, where you're like, "Oh my god, this is the perfect position."  And we couldn't implement any of them.  And you ask yourself, “What’s the problem with third tries?  We play great on the first and second.  But not very well on the third."  And I think it all comes down to our overall style of play; we should showcase it on video.  We have to show our physicality, the style of play that we want people to see on tape and say, "Yeah, this team plays really, really hard."  And then we have to do our job better. And on every attempt.    Is there anything where you saw the level of physical play not being up to your standards? Uh, sometimes, you know, sometimes it happens.  And I think a lot of this really happened.  It's hard to play physically when you're losing positionally and falling back. Yes?  You can't because you become predictable.  We've already talked about this. So how do you play physically? Well, they're not stupid. Okay, what's next?  Well, second down and 15 yards.  It will probably be takeout.  Is it a screen or a pass?  They're...you know, tough races.  You 're releasing big players, and they probably don't take it seriously.  So this levels the game dynamics.  This deprives you of many tools.  And when you keep the game balanced within yards, now you can play in many different ways. So, it was more about the game situation that didn't allow you to act differently. I think the game situation dictated the conditions, I analyzed the last two games. You know, we were just losing positionally Maybe this isn't the best week for questions, because it was pretty tough on the field.  But how do you see Tyler's growth, second year, more football, reading the game, and what stage is Zach Wilson at now? Uh, you know, this process...it's not a straight line.  In this league, you can't go from A to B in a straight line.  He always declines. And, you know, what Tyler does exceptionally well is that after making mistakes, he very quickly realizes the reason and understands what needs to be done to fix them.  And, uh, you know, when a quarterback comes back from the field and tells you exactly what he saw, like on SportsCenter, well, then you know he really sees the field. And you know they made a mistake .  Okay, but now we have to move on, right?  This should not happen again and again, otherwise you will have problems. But, uh, that's what's most impressive, and of course, he did a lot of really good things too.    The Giants have thrown eight interceptions this year.  What can you say about their ability to take the ball away on offense? They, of course, did an outstanding job.  Uh, in the back line, making interceptions.  They act aggressively.  As we said, the level of blitz has increased. So they are really good.  They keep their sights on the quarterback.  They are doing well and they are strong athletes. Do you have a prediction for Carl Rummel's game? There is, but I'll keep it to myself.

title: Packers' Josh Jacobs sues to block release of video of altercation | Pro Football Talk
text: The Green Bay Packers will play Sunday night without Josh Jacobs, who remains on the commissioner's exempt list, a fancy name for paid leave.  This will be the sixth game.  It has been thought that perhaps after six games he will return and , if he is ultimately suspended, he will be credited for the games he missed. Six is ​​the base number for a suspension due to a domestic violence situation.  He pleaded "no contentre" for assault after an incident on May 23, and since he had cameras in his home, they captured video of the altercation that resulted in that plea.  The NFL wants to see the video.  The public wants to see the video. It is a matter of public interest. How important is that public interest?  I don't know, but at least it's easy to argue that it's something that should interest the public because he's a player on a publicly owned team .  That would be true on any team, but he's on a publicly owned team in Green Bay. There is definitely greater public interest, but the NFL has a specific interest in seeing this evidence to correctly decide what the punishment should be.  And it's important that the NFL sees it before deciding, because of what happened in 2014 with Ray Rice. The NFL suspended him for two games, and the day after the regular season began, after the first Sunday, chaos erupted because TMZ obtained the video.  Then, the AP reported that the NFL had the video before TMZ, and the commissioner spent, I would say, 7 to 10 days wondering whether he would have to resign or be fired over this situation, which turned into a gigantic disaster for the NFL. They don't want that to happen again. They want to see that video.  So, the development since the show ended is that Josh Jacobs filed a lawsuit seeking a court order to prevent the video from being released. And the arguments presented make sense at first glance.  It seeks to protect the victim's identity.  Even if the face is blurred, there is enough information for artificial intelligence not to want to be considered the enemy.  Superintelligence could discern the victim's identity .  And this is a legitimate concern of Josh Jacobs.  The video shows some details of his garage.    It could allow thieves, by knowing when you are not in town, to identify your house, which one to attack, and so on.  But it also has the practical effect of preventing the NFL from seeing the video.  And I think, on some level, he wants to prevent the NFL from seeing the video.  And the NFL's answer should be very simple.  You don't play until we see the video.  And there must be a way to draft a court order that allows the NFL to have the video, on the condition that it cannot be disclosed.  It may only be used for internal purposes, with the objective of determining the appropriate punishment according to the personal conduct policy.  And it cannot be revealed to anyone else.  That would be very easy to do.  It seems Jacobs doesn't want the NFL to see the video, and that would lead any reasonable person to conclude that the video could do to his career what the Ray Rice video did to his.  Because Rice never played again after that video came out.  There is a difference between knowing what happened and seeing it.  So Jacobs risks the NFL saying, "Well, you're simply not going to play until we see the video." Well, if he knows that if they see the video he won't play anyway, his last effort, his desperate move, is to say: "Hey, referee. Hey, referee. Don't let them see the video."  I think the video should be available to the NFL at least, at the very least.  With appropriate safeguards against public disclosure.  They need to see it to make a good decision about whether Josh Jacobs will be suspended for six games, more, less, or whatever, or permanently banned.  The ultimate punishment under the personal conduct policy is a permanent ban with the possibility of applying for reinstatement after one year. Although in the end, public relations takes over.  If this comes to light, he becomes, depending on what he shows, but if it's something like Ray Rice's video, he becomes untouchable.  And that's the end of it .  Okay, I'm Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Subscribe to receive the latest news and analysis from Pro Football Talk.
